  3. The ECMAScript runtime (src/engine/jsrt)

#The ECMAScript runtime (src/engine/jsrt)

The runtime is the "second half" of Wren's Odin JavaScript engine: it executes QuickJS‑ng 0.17 bytecode. It is written natively in Odin, builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32 with an injected allocator and no OS dependency, and runs inside Wren's Wasm sandbox exactly as QuickJS‑in‑Wasm does (the sandbox is kept on purpose: it protects the host from memory bugs of the engine).

The two halves of the engine meet at the QuickJS‑ng 0.17 bytecode: the Odin front‑end (frontend.md) and the reference QuickJS C compiler emit the same serialized form, and this runtime reads and runs it. compile_frontend.odin calls the front‑end in process (a scratch arena per compile), so eval, Function(...), modules and $262.evalScript need no other compiler.

This is not a mechanical port of QuickJS. Where the C uses #define tags, manual refcounting and hand‑rolled dispatch, the Odin version uses tagged unions with exhaustive switch, defer, arenas where they help, comptime‑generated opcode/atom tables, and layouts friendly to #soa. Divergences are deliberate and listed at the end.

#Conformance (test262)

wrentool engine test262 builds the judge (src/engine/jsrt/judge) and runs the suite pinned by src/tools/test262 in worker processes (a crash or hang costs one test), with the rules of QuickJS‑ng's test262.conf. The harness files and the includes / flags of each test's front matter are honoured (onlyStrict, raw, async, module, CanBlockIsFalse); $262 provides createRealm, evalScript, detachArrayBuffer, gc, IsHTMLDDA and real agents (threads with their own runtime, sharing SharedArrayBuffer memory; Atomics.wait/notify go through a process‑wide waiter list).

#Value model (value.odin)

A Value is a 16‑byte tagged union: an 8‑bit Tag plus an 8‑byte payload (int32, float64, bool or a pointer to a GC cell). A tagged union rather than NaN‑boxing, on purpose:

  • It is identical on 64‑bit native and on wasm32; every switch v.tag is checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler.
  • Small integers stay unboxed (int32, as QuickJS); -0, non‑integral and out‑of‑range numbers use the float64 lane.

Heap values (string, symbol, object, bigint, raw function bytecode, module) hold a ^Cell. The representation is isolated behind constructors/accessors. The C API layer (below) encodes a Value in the 64‑bit NaN‑boxed word QuickJS uses on wasm32, because Wren's glue is written against that.

#Strings, atoms, shapes, objects

  • Strings (string.odin): UTF‑16 code units stored compactly — Latin‑1 (one byte per unit) or UTF‑16 — with ropes for concatenation (a + b + c… in a loop is linear; flattened on first index/hash/compare). Source text handed to the compiler keeps lone surrogates (WTF‑8), and Function.prototype.toString returns the real source text (the front‑end keeps each function's text with Compile_Options.keep_source; Host_Config.strip_source drops it).
  • Atoms (atom.odin, atoms_table.odin): 32‑bit interned property keys; array indices set bit 31 and never allocate. The predefined atoms are generated from quickjs-atom.h, so serialized bytecode refers to the same indices. Atoms are never collected.
  • Shapes (shape.odin/object.odin): hidden classes with transitions and an open‑addressed hash; an object stores a flat []Prop_Slot; deleting a property or growing past 48 properties switches the object to a private dictionary shape.
  • Objects: a GC cell with a shape, inline slots, and an Object_Data tagged union for the internal slots of exotic kinds (Array, Function, Native, Bound, wrappers, ArrayBuffer/TypedArray/DataView, Map/Set, Proxy, Date, RegExp, Promise, Generator, Module namespace, Host…). Arrays keep a dense []Value fast path.
  • The layout on wasm32, what ships (#asserted in object.odin): a Cell header is 8 bytes (size; the kind in a nibble with pinned, in_ext and two bits of the kind's own in a byte; mark a byte; the host's count of references in 16 bits, which sticks at its top and makes the cell a root for good); an Object 40 (a native function's magic in it, so that Object_Data is 16, the size of its largest variant); a string header 28, a closure cell (Var_Ref) 32 (detached when pvalue points at its own value). An object's slots follow it in its cell when it is made with them (object_new_shape: an empty plain object has room for 4, one of a known shape exactly its keys), and so do what was out of line and lives as long as the object: a closure's cells (object_tail), an iterator's state, the values of an array, of an arguments object or of a match made with their room (array_like_new, up to a block of the pool). Slots or values that grow past it take a block of their own; what was in the cell stays there, unused. A plain object is 104 bytes, a closure 72 with its two cells, [a, b] 88, in one block each.
  • A function's prototype is made when something first reads, defines or describes it (Prop_Kind.lazy_prototype, function_prototype_make): the slot is empty and the property's kind says so, every path that looks at a property's value goes by its kind, and the object then takes the shape the same keys have as data properties. An assignment (F.prototype = {...}) makes no object first (function_prototype_settle).

#Memory management (gc.odin)

A precise, non‑moving, stop‑the‑world mark‑and‑sweep collector. Copying a Value is a plain copy: there are no dup/free pairs in the interpreter and cycles need no special pass.

  • Where the cells are, and their marks. A cell of the pool (≤ 512 bytes) is known by two bits of its chunk (Chunk_Bits, one pair of words per 32 grains of 8 bytes, after the chunk's header): one says a cell starts there, the other that it is marked. A cell finds its chunk by Runtime.chunk_table, the chunk of each 4 KiB of the addresses (chunks start on 4 KiB and are made of them: aligned on their own 256 KiB, the Wasm allocator lost up to that much in front of each). A cell is made marked, and a marking starts by clearing every mark: outside a marking, a cell that lives is marked (cell_marked). A cell over 512 bytes has its mark in its header and is listed (Runtime.big_cells). The bits cost 1/32 of a chunk; the list of every cell they replace cost 4 bytes a cell.
  • The sweep reads the bits, not the cells: a group of 32 grains whose cells all live is one load, a cell that lives is never touched; a dead one is finalized if it owns anything (cell_alone: a plain object with its slots inline, a closure, a flat string, a closure cell do not) and freed at once. It goes chunk by chunk, in the order of the addresses, in steps after the marking (gc_sweep_step: 1 MiB of chunks for each 128 KiB allocated since the last step), the big cells last. So no finalizer reads another cell: a function's closure cells are always in its own cell (function_refs), and a Map or Set iterator that dies unfinished gives its map back the right to compact at the marking (gc_release_map_iters), not in its finalizer.
  • Roots: realms, the interpreter frame chain (arguments, locals, whole operand stacks, open closure cells), the job queue, the pending exception, atoms, the module registry, temp_roots, and the host roots (below).
  • Safe points (function entry, loop back edge, entry of a native call) are the only places a collection starts; allocation never collects. Native code (builtins) keeps Values in Odin locals the collector cannot see; cell_new and get/call push what they return on temp_roots, which a native call truncates when it returns. Builtins that read straight out of internal storage and then call back into JS root explicitly (root).
  • Weak references (WeakMap/WeakSet keys, WeakRef, FinalizationRegistry) are ephemerons processed to a fixpoint after the strong marking; shape transition caches are weak too.
  • Host roots: each Cell has a 32‑bit ext count. persist/ext_ref bump it (O(1), no table), unpersist/ext_unref drop it; cells with a non‑zero count are listed in rt.ext_cells and are roots.
  • Host classes (host_class.odin): objects of a class the host registers carry an opaque pointer, a finalizer, and optionally the references the opaque data holds (gc_mark) and exotic hooks for properties the object does not store. Finalizers of dead host objects run before any cell of the collection is freed. gc_mark is used twice: to subtract those references from the host counts (a cycle through opaque data does not keep itself alive — QuickJS's trial deletion, restricted to the cells with host references) and to trace them when the owner is live. The host part of such an object is a block of the size classes below, which may hold the opaque data itself (payload: the glue's wrappers), freed with it. Only the objects listed in rt.gc_hooked are asked (host_object_set_marked): one made with a payload is listed when its host says its data holds a value.
  • Small blocks (≤ 512 bytes: cells, inline slots, small arrays and string data) come from size‑class free lists carved out of 256 KiB chunks of the injected allocator (mem_alloc / mem_free / mem_resize in gc.odin; callers always pass the size they allocated with). A cell costs a pop and a push, not a host allocation.
  • The heap is capped by Host_Config.malloc_limit; all allocation goes through the injected allocator. A collection runs when the heap passes max(2.5 × live, live + 4 MiB).
  • Runtime.gc_swept counts the cells freed and kept (kept: counted from the bits, not read); Runtime.gc_ns the time of the markings and sweeps (judge eval prints it); -define:JSRT_GC_CENSUS=true counts what died by kind, as the census of the heap does (Runtime.gc_dead, jsengine mem, WREN_JS_MEMPROF=1: the census of a window's realm at its load event).
  • The strings of numbers made lately (str_from_u64: n.toString(), an index as a key) are kept in 256 slots until the next collection clears them: a page that makes the same number a string for each element of a list makes it once. Such a string (STR_NUMBER) joined to a constant of the code, or to another, is kept too (Runtime.concat_strings, 256 slots, cleared the same way): t.toString() + ":true" for each element is one string.

#Allocations nothing sees

Each falls back to the general path wherever the protocol can be seen; examples/jsbench/hotcheck.js checks each way.

  • for…of and array destructuring over Array.prototype.values (an array, arguments, a NodeList): when the object's @@iterator is this realm's values and %ArrayIteratorPrototype%.next is still the built-in data property, for_of_start leaves the object and an index on the operand stack in place of the iterator and its next (for_of_fast), and for_of_next steps them as the iterator would, its length read again at each step (array_values_at). A close (a break, a return, a throw, a destructuring that leaves elements) makes the iterator and calls its return only if %ArrayIteratorPrototype% or what it inherits from may have one (a proxy, a host object, lazy members: asked) (for_of_close). yield* keeps its iterator.
  • A mapped arguments object's closure cells are in its own cell when nothing else can hold them: no function inside captures an argument, no direct eval, no coroutine (mapped_args_in_cell, found once a function, kept in its bytecode's cell flags). The frame lists them as its own (it closes them at its return), and an open one keeps its object alive (Var_Ref.owner).
  • Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(o, p).field read at once (the interpreter's hot loop: the call followed by get_field): the field, without the descriptor; a field the descriptor would not have makes it (descriptor_field).
  • Object.defineProperty(o, p, {value: v, enumerable: !0, ...}), a literal of loads and constants handed to the call: its fields go to the descriptor without the object, unless Object.prototype has a field the literal does not (hot_define_literal, define_property_literal).

#Where the memory of a realm and of a page goes (Wasm, jsengine mem|startup)

The linear memory of a Wasm module only grows, so what counts is the high-water mark.

  • Lazy members. A Web IDL prototype (native/js/odin/wj/qjs_platform.odin, wj_platform_preinit) is marked lazy with JS_SetLazyMembers: its shape is private and flagged, and shape_find, the enumerations of a shape (own_property_keys, plain_keys_object) and add_property call shape_realize first, which runs the glue's callback (lazy_proto_members): it defines the members the eager code defined, with the same keys, order, descriptors, names and lengths, minus what the realm's scope hides and the touch handlers browser.touch.expose turned off, plus the unimplemented-throw members after the implemented ones. A realm creates the thousands of function objects of the interfaces a script looks at, not all of them. A prototype that pre-initialization touches after the members (iterator interfaces) is realized in the image. The interface objects, namespaces and the global object stay eager. Empty realm: 6 592 → 4 352 KiB of linear memory, 6 973 → 4 723 KiB private per realm, 2.3 → 1.3 ms to create.
  • Native functions. A function object has exactly the two slots (length, name) it is born with; a C function of the glue without user data keeps its pointer in Native_Data.data (low bit set, native_data_is_raw) and its prototype in which bridge_* procedure it calls (no block of values); its name is the string of the property key's atom when there is one (str_interned).
  • The compiler (compile_alloc.odin): the front-end's allocator takes blocks up to 2 KiB from the arena, recycles them by size class (a larger free block is cut for a smaller request), and takes larger ones from the host heap, one by one, so that a table that dies is given back at once. js_create_function frees a function's tables (free_func_def) as soon as its bytecode exists, the passes free their buffers, and the serialized stream is built in one buffer (serialize.odin). The 650 KiB bundle of examples/jsbench/page_gen.js asked the arena for 14.6 MB, now 6.5.

#Serialized‑bytecode reader and verifier (serialize.odin)

Parses the stream of the front‑end, BC_VERSION 29: QuickJS's JS_WriteObject(..., JS_WRITE_OBJ_BYTECODE) (28) but for a function's record, which is a head (flags, name, counts, position, closure variables without their names) and a body with its length in front (closure names, cpool, vardefs, bytecode, line table, source). Also the atom table (both atom encodings of the format), BigInt, arrays, objects, modules.

Most functions of a page never run, so a function is read in two steps. read_object keeps the stream (Bytecode_Store, shared by the functions read from it, freed with the last of them; JS_WriteObject hands it out), goes over the atom table noting where each atom is, and reads the top‑level function, head and body. A head is read with its parent's cpool; a body, and with it the heads of the functions it holds, at the function's first run. An atom is read at its first use. Until then the function's code is LAZY_CODE, one instruction (lazy_body, past OPCODE_COUNT: no stream can hold it) that reads the body and starts the frame again: every way into a function ends there, and a call pays nothing for it. The JIT reads the body itself at its entry when its threshold is 1, and does not compile or inline what has not run. Function.prototype.toString reads the body. The line table and the source stay in the stream.

Once a body is read, the atom operands of its code (a copy) are rewritten and a stack‑height verifier checks it. The interpreter trusts the types of operands (as QuickJS does: bytecode comes from the compiler); the reader and verifier guarantee shape and stack discipline, not type correctness. A stream that fails: read_object throws for the top‑level function (the browser then compiles the source); a nested function throws a SyntaxError at each of its calls.

#Interpreter (interp.odin, ops.odin, coro.odin)

A switch‑dispatch loop over the QuickJS instruction set. The common instructions (locals, arguments, integer / float arithmetic, comparisons, branches, get_field / put_field with the prototype walk, array reads and writes, global variables through a per‑realm slot cache, string constants, calls and returns, and the native getter of an accessor that get_field or a global finds: a DOM attribute, window.document) run in interp_hot.odin, a loop with raw pointers whose few live values stay in registers; everything else, and every fast path that does not apply, leaves it with the pc on the instruction for the full dispatch in interp.odin. The hot loop is inlined into interp_run (measured: a separate procedure is 20‑25 % slower). Frames come from segmented value stacks so generators and async functions can suspend them (coro.odin: generators, async functions, async generators, for await, yield*). A plain JS‑to‑JS call does not recurse natively: frame_push puts the callee's Frame at the end of its value‑stack block and the same interp_run activation runs it (Frame.stackless), and so does new of a bytecode function, a spread call and a getter or a setter a property instruction finds (Stackless: what the frame's return gives its caller); native callees (c_function) are called from the hot loop without a frame. What goes through a native (map, a Proxy trap, Reflect, a bound function, a listener) takes a new interp_run on the host stack. Host_Config.max_stack_depth bounds all of it, with a RangeError at the limit. On Wasm the host stack is two stacks (stack.odin): the shadow stack in linear memory is 2 MiB, every page of which is committed for each realm, and a recursion that runs past it goes on in blocks of the heap (the host moves the stack pointer, Engine_stackMove; the blocks go when the outermost call returns); the machine's stack ends in a trap, so the engine asks the host (Engine_nativeStackLow) at each move and at each entry of the browser into a running engine, and stops with the same RangeError. Natively, one stack and Host_Config.max_stack_bytes. The interrupt hook runs on a budget from the loop back edge. Operators follow the spec (+ through ToPrimitive, ModRing bitwise, BigInt paths, loose and strict equality). Try/catch uses a per‑frame handler stack (catch/gosub/ret/nip_catch).

#Standard library

Everything QuickJS‑ng 0.17 ships, in b_*.odin: Object, Function, Array, String (with Unicode case mapping and normalization from src/engine/unicode), Number/Math/BigInt (numconv, bigint), Symbol, JSON (with source text access), RegExp, Date (datetime), Map/Set/WeakMap/WeakSet/WeakRef/ FinalizationRegistry, Promise, generators, Reflect/Proxy, ArrayBuffer (resizable, immutable)/ SharedArrayBuffer (growable)/TypedArray/Float16Array/DataView/Atomics, Iterator helpers and Iterator.concat, Array.fromAsync, DisposableStack/AsyncDisposableStack/SuppressedError, Uint8Array base64/hex, Error.prototype.stack. Intl stays on the host (Wren's glue).

Regular expressions. Literals reach the runtime already compiled by the front‑end to the bytecode of QuickJS's libregexp; lre_exec.odin executes that format (and a verifier checks it before use), so literals and new RegExp share one matcher. Unicode properties, case folding and the properties of strings (\p{RGI_Emoji} …) come from tables generated from the pinned UCD. The matcher recognises a greedy loop of one character (\S+, [^"]*, .*) as the compiler emits it and takes the run at once, with one state of the kind .run for all of its positions, the character that follows the loop tried before it goes back to a position (the format does not change, and a subject read as code points takes the bytecode's way). A search whose regexp starts with such a run, without back references, goes on after the run when it fails: what follows was tried at every position a later start could reach, so /\S+@\S+\.\S+/ on a long token is linear where backtracking is quadratic.

#Embedding interface (embed.odin, runtime.odin)

engine_new / context_new / eval_source / eval_bytecode / call_function / run_jobs / retain / release / heap_stats, with the hooks in Host_Config: compile, load_module, import_meta, interrupt, rejection, gc_prologue, gc_epilogue, compile_strings, dynamic_import, atomics_wait/atomics_notify, can_block, malloc_limit. Values handed to the host live until the next call into the engine unless retained.

src/engine/jsrt/wasm is the freestanding module (jsrt_init/new/alloc/eval/run_jobs/free).

#The QuickJS C API on this runtime (src/engine/jscapi)

Wren's glue is written against quickjs.h. jscapi implements that API (167 procedures, proc "c", exported under their QuickJS names with -define:JSCAPI_EXPORT=true) over jsrt; see jscapi.md for the ownership model, the classes and the plan of what is left.

JSRT_PROF=1 judge eval is a sampling profiler (hot functions and source lines; build the judge with -debug). JSRT_MEMPROF=1 on judge eval prints a census of the heap by kind of cell (count, cell bytes, bytes owned out of line, slack; memprof.odin), jsengine mem [-image m.wasm] file.js does the same inside the wasm32 image (sizes of the cells on wasm32, linear memory of the module, which only grows), and WREN_JS_MEMPROF=1 makes the jsdom web tests print it for each page. examples/jsbench/page_gen.js generates a 650 KB framework-like bundle for page-load memory (the compile arena dominates it). Timings on this machine swing by ±30 % from run to run when other builds are running, and a change that adds no work to the hot loop can still move an unrelated case by ±10 % (code layout), so compare interleaved and keep the best. Fuzzing: judge fuzz <dir> mutates serialized bytecode and loads it (reader + verifier; 40 000 mutants, no crash; running accepted mutants is opt‑in with JSRT_FUZZ_RUN=1, since a type‑confused image can crash any interpreter that trusts the compiler); judge fuzzsrc <dir> mutates source text, compiles with the Odin front‑end and runs under an interrupt budget (30 000 mutants on language/ and built-ins/, no crash).

#Intended divergences from QuickJS

  • Tagged union over NaN‑boxing for values; precise tracing GC instead of reference counting plus a cycle collector (the C API layer re‑creates the counted‑reference contract for the glue).
  • Exhaustive Odin enums + switch for tags, exotic kinds and opcodes; comptime‑generated opcode and atom tables from the QuickJS headers.
  • Rope strings with Latin‑1/UTF‑16 compaction as the default string representation.
  • Atoms are permanent; JS_WriteObject of data (structured clone format) is not implemented.

#Known gaps

The 34 test262 failures above (all shared with QuickJS‑ng). Speed is at parity with QuickJS on the micro benchmarks; the slow cases are the ones that pay one dispatch per bytecode (switch on integers 62 %, nested integer loops 69 %: next step is superinstructions or a pre‑decoded code array), native‑to‑JS callbacks (sort comparators, forEach: a new interp_run activation each, ~1.9× slower than QuickJS) and destructuring. Memory is 1.4× QuickJS on allocation‑heavy scripts (natively a plain object costs 136 bytes; on wasm32, what ships, 104: Object 40 + 4 inline slots of 16; a string header is 28 bytes; what is left is mostly the 16 bytes of a Value).
